title: Seating Repair
pitch: A WebMCP workspace for repairing constrained plans while keeping humans in control
about_excerpt: A WebMCP workspace for repairing constrained plans while keeping humans in control Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A surprising number of everyday operational problems are really placement problems in disguise. You have a set of people, tasks, items, vehicles, or events, a limited number of places or resources, and a collection of rules that determine what can go where. We see this everywhere. Guests need to be assigned to tables. Patients need beds. Employees need shifts. Classes need rooms. Aircraft need gates. Jobs need machines. Inventory needs storage locations. In every case, the basic question is the same: how do you put the right thing in the right place while respecting all the constraints around it? Creating the first plan is only part of the challenge. The harder part often comes later, when reality changes after the plan has already been accepted. A guest suddenly needs an accessible table. Two people can no longer sit together. A VIP needs a specific position. A resource becomes unavailable. A manager makes a last-minute decision that should not be undone. At that point, the goal is not to throw everything away and optimize from scratch. It is to repair the existing plan while preserving as much of what already works as possible. Traditional optimization systems are good at solving structured problems, but people do not usually describe operational changes as formal constraints. They say things like "keep these two apart", "do not move this person", or "this group needs to stay together". An AI agent can help translate that kind of natural-language intent into structured constraints, but there is another problem: the agent may be working from an older version of the plan while a person is still editing the live page. That creates a very real failure mode. A person can make an important manual change, and the agent can later overwrite it simply because it is still acting on stale state. We wanted to explore a collaboration model where that cannot happen silently. We chose seating because it makes the larger idea easy to see. A guest represents an entity that needs to be assigned. A table represents a limited-capacity resource. "Together" and "apart" rules behave like clustering constraints. Accessibility and fixed-table rules represent eligibility and placement requirements. A locked guest represents a human decision that the agent is not allowed to override. Seating Repair is our way of exploring how WebMCP can bring these pieces together: natural-language agency, deterministic constraint solving, live application state, and direct human control, all operating on the same shared planning surface. What it does Seating Repair is a WebMCP application for solving and repairing constrained placement problems while a person and an agent are both working on the same live plan. The demo uses 12 fictional guests and three tables because that makes the idea easy to understand at a glance. But underneath the seating interface, the application is dealing with a more general planning problem: limited-capacity resources, people who must stay together or apart, fixed placements, eligibility requirements such as accessibility, decisions that a human has explicitly locked, and the need to keep as much of the existing plan unchanged as possible. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can read the exact current state of the board, understand the active constraints, add new hard constraints from a person's request, repair the plan, and then validate the result. The goal is not simply to press an "optimize" button and generate a completely new seating arrangement. In a real planning workflow, many existing decisions are already correct and should stay that way. A useful repair needs to preserve what still works, respect every hard constraint, treat human-locked placements as authoritative, change only what is necessary, and verify that the final result is actually valid. This becomes especially important when a person and an agent are working at the same time. If the agent reads the board and a person then moves or locks a guest, the agent is no longer allowed to write using the old version of the plan. That stale write is rejected with STATE_CHANGED. The agent has to read the page again and continue from the decision the person actually made instead of silently overwriting it. In the demo, this is easy to see: a person can move Grandma Rose to a different table and lock her there. The agent can then add another constraint, repair the remaining conflicts, and validate the board while leaving Grandma Rose exactly where the person placed her. Seating is the domain we chose to demonstrate the idea, but it is not the limit of the underlying pattern. The same kind of constrained allocation and repair appears in restaurant and event operations, protocol seating, workforce scheduling, room and resource allocation, patient-to-bed assignment, airport gate reassignment, and many other situations where a working plan has to adapt as constraints and human decisions change. The current build is intentionally focused on demonstrating that shared coordination model clearly. It is not meant to pretend that one seating demo is already a complete product for every one of those industries. Instead, it shows the core interaction pattern: an AI agent can help repair a constrained plan, while the live application remains the source of truth and human decisions remain in control. How we built it We built Seating Repair as a lightweight TypeScript app with Vite. Everything runs in the browser, with no backend and no separate database for the agent. The seating board that the person sees is the same state the WebMCP tools work with. We kept the WebMCP side intentionally simple and exposed only four tools. One reads the current seating state, one adds hard constraints, one repairs the plan, and one validates the result. That was enough to cover the full interaction we wanted to demonstrate without turning the project into a large collection of overlapping tools. We also did not want the language model itself to be responsible for deciding whether a seating plan is correct. The agent can understand a request such as "keep these two apart" or "do not move this guest", but the actual planning is handled by deterministic application code. The repair logic runs in the browser and searches for an arrangement that satisfies all of the current constraints. It checks table capacity, together and apart rules, fixed-table requirements, accessibility, and human locks. When there is more than one valid solution, it prefers one that changes as little of the current plan as possible. Human edits are treated as first-class state changes. A person can move a guest manually and lock that placement. Once a guest is locked, the agent cannot move them during a repair. There is no hidden tool option that lets the agent ignore the lock; the person has to unlock that guest first. One of the main things we wanted to get right was what happens when the human changes the board while the agent is working. Every change to the seating plan increments a revision number. When the agent tries to change the plan, it has to provide the revision it previously read. If the board has changed since then, the write is rejected with STATE_CHANGED. That means the agent cannot quietly apply an old plan over a newer human decision. It has to read the current board again and continue from there. Repairs are also atomic. The solver works on a snapshot first and only updates the live board after it has found a complete valid solution. If the constraints cannot be satisfied, the current plan stays as it was instead of being left in a partially changed state. The manual UI and the WebMCP tools share the same store, validation logic, and constraint model. We wanted there to be one source of truth rather than one version of the plan for the person and another version for the agent. For the demo, state is stored in browser localStorage, which keeps the project self-contained. We also added tests for the behaviors we considered most important: constraint validation, deterministic repairs, minimum-change solutions, human locks, unsatisfiable plans, stale revisions, invalid tool input, and WebMCP tool execution. The overall design is fairly simple on purpose: the agent handles natural-language intent, WebMCP gives it structured access to the live application, and normal deterministic code is still responsible for enforcing the rules and deciding whether the final plan is valid. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not the seating solver itself. It was deciding how a person and an agent should safely work on the same plan without one silently undoing the other. At first, it is tempting to treat the agent like a normal automation flow: read the state, calculate a better arrangement, and write the result back.
